001-250203:
The applicant, Samet Kaya, a Turkish national born in 1993 and living in Ankara, lodged application no. 42109/22 against Türkiye on 11 August 2022. He complained under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention about his dismissal by the Council of Judges and Prosecutors (HSK) on the basis of a Forensic Medicine Institute (FMI) report concluding that he was unfit on health grounds to carry out judicial or prosecutorial duties.

The applicant graduated from a Turkish law faculty. After passing a judicial candidate exam on 3 June 2017 and an oral interview, he was selected on 28 July 2017 as a candidate for judicial or prosecutorial office. He was appointed prosecutor in Karabük and took up his functions on 5 November 2018. He was married at the time but divorced shortly afterwards.

In April 2019 the applicant reported personal difficulties after his divorce and took sick leave. On 25 April 2019 he was diagnosed with depression at Ankara Kahramankazan State Hospital and began medication. On 29 April 2019, while at the courthouse, he suffered a nervous breakdown and was taken to Karabük University Hospital. Records noted insomnia, severe uneasiness and restlessness, disorganised behaviour, impaired judgment, paranoid persecutory delusions, suicidal thoughts, difficulty being calmed, an attempt to leave the emergency department, and unusual behaviour involving a dog. On 30 April 2019 he was diagnosed with a “schizophrenia-like acute psychotic disorder” and admitted as an inpatient. On 8 May 2019 he was discharged against medical advice. He then sought treatment at Ankara University Gülhane Training and Research Hospital, where he was admitted on 9 May 2019 with a diagnosis of “psychosis”. By 27 May 2019 active psychopathology was no longer observed; he was discharged for outpatient treatment with one month’s medical leave, a reference to “anxiety disorder”, and a recommendation for psychiatric consultation every two weeks.

After his leave, the HSK appointed him judge rapporteur at the Court of Cassation, at his request, to facilitate treatment in Ankara; he began in June 2019. He remarried on 27 December 2019. On 17 June 2020, at his request and on family grounds, the HSK appointed him prosecutor in Hatay.

On 25 June 2019 his medical reports were sent to the HSK’s Professional Admission Office to inquire whether his health precluded judicial service. On 17 September 2019 the HSK Second Chamber sought an expert report on whether his condition prevented continuous performance of judicial or prosecutorial duties anywhere in the country. On 3 October 2019 it requested his referral to the FMI. He was examined six times by the FMI Fourth Specialised Board between 29 November 2019 and 26 May 2021.

On 11 August 2021 the FMI reported to the HSK. It found “no significant psychopathology” and that the applicant was “still in remission” under treatment, but gave decisive weight to the severity of his initial diagnoses and the risk of stress-related recurrence. It unanimously concluded he could not continuously perform judicial or prosecutorial duties nationwide. On 7 September 2021 the HSK Second Chamber terminated his duties, finding he had lost qualifications under section 8(g) of Law no. 2802.

On 10 September 2021 a Hatay University Hospital report found no active psychopathology impairing his capacity or preventing his duties and concluded he had fully recovered. On 16 September 2021 he submitted it to the HSK, sought review, argued there had been no recurrence over about two and a half years and no adverse effects on professional or private life, and asked for a higher FMI board. On 5 October 2021 the HSK accepted review and referred him to the FMI High Board. On 14 December 2021 the First High Board re-examined him; while noting no significant psychopathology and continued remission, it reiterated the historical diagnosis and potential stress-related recurrence, and unanimously found him unsuitable. On 28 December 2021 the Second Chamber dismissed his review request.

The applicant objected to the HSK Plenary, submitting a second Hatay University Hospital report dated 9 March 2022 reiterating full recovery. He also alleged a procedural flaw: that the HSK was required to conduct a preliminary investigation into actual professional performance before referring him to the FMI. The Plenary dismissed the objection on 6 April 2022, notified on 9 May 2022. Under domestic law, HSK decisions other than dismissals for misconduct are not subject to judicial review; objections to the Plenary are final.
001-250211:
The applicant, Viktor Sergiyovych Kovalenko, a Ukrainian national born in 1985 living in Bucha, was represented by lawyer G.V. Tokarev. The Government of Ukraine were represented by their Agent, Ms Marharyta Sokorenko. The application concerned alleged ill-treatment of the applicant on 17 February 2008 and an alleged lack of effective investigation.

According to the applicant, on 17 February 2008 at about 10 p.m. he, his friend B. and their girlfriends Ya. and S. were near the entrance to a multi-storey building in which his flat was located. A group of young men attacked them. Two attackers were off-duty police officers from the Irpin police station, investigators M.B. and K. One struck the applicant’s head with an expandable metal baton. The applicant tried to defend himself with a pocketknife and sustained injuries, including head trauma and brief loss of consciousness. M.B. and K. initiated his arrest, called the patrol, and the applicant and B. were taken to the Irpin police station, where the applicant was allegedly forced to sign a statement that he and B. had started the fight for hooligan motives.

The Government submitted that at about 9 p.m. the applicant and B. started a fight with off-duty police officers. The applicant used a penknife, inflicting stab wounds on M.B. and injuries on O.B. and B.Ye. The police arrived after a witness called. The Government stated that the applicant sustained only light injuries and did not seek medical assistance, but did not provide copies of forensic reports for M.B., O.B. or B.Ye. On 18 February 2008 at 12.10 a.m., the applicant and B. underwent blood-alcohol testing, each showing 0.6%; M.B. was sober. No other person was tested.

On 20 February 2008 forensic doctor I. classified the applicant’s injuries as minor and advised neurological examination. On 22 February 2008 he was admitted to Irpin Hospital and discharged on 3 March 2008 with diagnoses including closed head injury, concussion and cervical contusion. On 4 March 2008 he was hospitalised at Kyiv Regional Clinical Hospital; a CT scan on 5 March 2008 led doctor Go. to conclude he had a parietal bone fracture. He was discharged on 13 March 2008 with a final diagnosis including closed head injury, right parietal fracture and cervical contusion. Later forensic assessments in 2009 disputed or downplayed skull/brain injury, while a 25 April 2016 examination concluded the skull fracture was serious. On 18 March 2013 a criminal case was opened against forensic doctor I. for an allegedly untrue expert conclusion; it was closed on 26 April 2021 for lack of evidence.

On 16 May 2012 the Irpin prosecutor’s office reported that the original applicant’s medical file had been lost after transfer from the Irpin Bureau of Forensic Medical Examination to the Borodyanka prosecutor’s office. Officer I.I. had received it on 7 May 2009. In 2013 witnesses were questioned in a criminal case into official negligence.

Domestically, on 18 February 2008 a criminal case was opened against the applicant and B. for hooliganism; they signed self-incriminating statements and later retracted them, alleging duress. On 20 July 2008 the Irpin City Court reversed the decision opening that case, upheld on 10 September 2008. From 2008 to 2011 prosecutors repeatedly refused to open a case into the applicant’s ill-treatment; domestic courts overturned those refusals as unlawful or premature, citing failures to question patrol officers and K., verify the baton, test other participants for alcohol, assess the off-duty officers’ actions, and verify duress complaints. On 18 July 2014 criminal case no. 12014110040001203 was opened into injuries to the applicant, B. and Ya.; it was transferred to the Kyiv regional prosecutor’s office. The case was closed for lack of evidence on 28 May 2019, that closure was overturned on 8 August 2023, and the proceedings were closed again on 1 March 2024.

Separate criminal proceedings against on-duty police officers who detained the applicant were opened on 13 March 2015, closed in 2015 and 2019, and repeatedly overturned by domestic courts. In 2023 the case file was reported missing and an internal investigation was launched.
001-250214:
The applicant, Ms Valentyna Pavlivna Buzyna, born in 1939, is the mother of Mr Oles Buzyna, a well-known author and journalist perceived as having pro-Russian views, who was shot dead near his home in Kyiv on 16 April 2015. On 3 August 2017 the applicant lodged an application concerning the investigation into the murder and the length of the related proceedings.

On the day of the murder, the crime scene and the victim’s body were inspected. A car used in the murder was found and seized; its examination and objects found in or around it ultimately allowed suspects M. and P. to be identified. Extensive investigative measures followed, including witness interviews, searches, and collection of biological samples and data from social networks and telecommunications operators.

In June 2015 M. and P. were arrested, and on 18 June 2015 the Kyiv Police Directorate charged them with murder. According to the charges, M. had been an officer in a volunteer police battalion attached to the Kyiv Police Directorate and had been a member of a nationalist political party from 28 March 2012 to 6 November 2014. P. belonged to another nationalist political party. They allegedly shared radical nationalist views and knew the victim’s social and political views. At the beginning of 2015 they allegedly conspired with unidentified persons to murder the victim because of hostility towards his views. They allegedly bought a firearm, described as an 1895 Nagant revolver, and in March 2015 bought an imported car registered in Italy. From 9 to 16 April 2015 they allegedly monitored the victim before shooting him on 16 April 2015. The defendants denied guilt throughout the proceedings.

Initially the investigation was conducted by the Kyiv Police Directorate. In October 2015 it was transferred to the prosecutor’s office because M. had been a member of the Ministry of the Interior’s armed unit. The applicant and the victim’s widow were recognised as aggrieved parties.

In November 2015 a court ordered Facebook and Skype to provide information and ordered a handwriting examination. In December 2015 the defendants were released and placed under house arrest, later lifted. On 10 December 2015 the court examined witnesses, some of whom testified to an alibi. Further court orders for evidence collection were issued in December 2015, January 2016 and April–July 2016. From 30 March 2016 to 22 June 2017 the investigation was repeatedly suspended to request information from the United States and Italy.

In August 2016 the applicant’s representative wrote to the prosecutor’s office, alleging that M. was a person of interest in another robbery case and that material indicated he had organised a surveillance group and sought untraceable SIM cards. The prosecutor’s office replied in September 2016 that the information would be verified. In October and November 2016 the representative asked the prosecutor’s office to investigate a Facebook post of 15 October 2016 by Mr V., which referred generally to the “murdered Buzyna the writer”. In December 2016 the prosecutor’s office replied that the investigation had been suspended.

On 27 June 2017 the pre-trial investigation concerning the defendants was completed, and in November 2017 the case was sent to the Kyiv Shevchenkivskyi District Court for trial. The Government stated that the defence lodged 184 complaints against investigating authorities, so the case was scheduled for examination only on 7 June 2018. From 23 October 2018 to 9 November 2021 the defence submitted 20 challenges to judges, jurors and prosecutors, voluminous inadmissibility applications and postponement requests. On 11 June 2019 the trial was restarted after a change of presiding judge. After 24 February 2022, hearings were adjourned in February, October and December 2022 for safety reasons or power cuts. On 11 April 2023 the hearing was adjourned because the defendants had been sent to the armed forces. Two jurors were released in August 2022 and April 2023 after reaching maximum age, and could not be replaced for some time; new jurors were pre-selected in May 2023. The trial court sought clarification from the Supreme Court, which replied on 16 September 2024. On 24 September 2024 the hearing was adjourned due to an air raid alert; the next hearing was scheduled for 4 December 2024.

In June 2017 a separate set of criminal proceedings was split off to investigate other possible individuals involved in the murder, entrusted to the State Bureau of Investigation. On 2 August 2021 the Prosecutor General’s Office issued directives to reactivate the investigation, including interviewing the victim’s mother and widow, collecting police and SBU information about operational-search activities concerning M., P. and two others, examining materials the applicant’s representative had referenced in 2016, and considering whether V. should be questioned. That investigation remained pending.
001-250216:
The application (no. 2091/22) was lodged on 29 December 2021 by Rastislav Trnka, a Slovak national born in 1984 who lives in Košice. He was represented by I. Rajtáková, a lawyer practising in Košice. The Slovak Government was represented by its Agent, M. Bálintová.

The case concerns a court order requiring the applicant, at the relevant time a member of a local council in a regional capital city, to apologise for statements made about another person and to pay that person EUR 3,000 in compensation. The other person was, at the relevant time, the mayor of that city and a member of the national parliament.

The statements were made on 30 January 2013 at a press conference called by the applicant, titled “The private company’s collection of parking fees will cut short [ukráti] Košice’s profits by EUR 50 million,” and were followed by a press release. They related to contracts under which the municipality had previously let public parking areas to a private party, with the aim that the party would operate a paid municipal public parking system in return for paying an annual lump sum to the municipality. The applicant believed the terms of those contracts were disadvantageous for the municipality.

In the impugned statements, the applicant said, among other things, that at the press conference he would present a carefully prepared con trick [podraz] on the citizens of Košice and the residents of the Old Town; that the Košice city administration was draining financial resources from the city budget, income and the pockets of citizens; that such a shady deal [kšeft] was probably not successful even during the Sh. era; that Košice was indeed the ECC but unfortunately also the European Capital of Shady Deals; that the mayor might be schizophrenic because in Bratislava he promoted the nationalisation of private companies, creating monopolies and imposing the theory that State ownership was best, but when he travelled 400 kilometres east he did the exact opposite; and that the current leadership of Košice had secured high profits for a private company which, according to the applicant’s calculations, would exceed EUR 50 million over ten years at the stated parking prices, with revenues of around EUR 60 million.

In an action for defamation brought by the mayor, the domestic courts analysed whether the applicant’s speech constituted value judgments or statements of fact and considered the opposing interests of the defendant and the claimant. The domestic courts emphasised that the applicant had to prove all of his allegations. They held that the applicant had failed to show that his statements were not statements of fact and referred to “untruthful value judgments” which should have been proved. For example, they stated that the applicant had not provided any evidence that the mayor was schizophrenic.

In a decision of 15 June 2021, notified to the applicant on 30 June 2021, the Constitutional Court dismissed a constitutional complaint brought by the applicant, noting the issue of non-exhaustion, in particular that the applicant had not referred in his complaint to the decision of the Supreme Court in his case. The Constitutional Court nevertheless reviewed the substance of his complaint.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained that his right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention had been violated.
001-250226:
The case comprises four applications against Ukraine: no. 38243/15 (Sergiy Kulish, b. 1947, lodged 27 July 2015); no. 8844/22 (Oleg Tsmokalov, b. 1975, lodged 28 January 2022, represented by O. Kornaga); no. 45988/22 (Lyudmyla Pereta, b. 1985, lodged 12 September 2022, represented by O. Kornaga); and no. 10629/24 (Anatoliy Broznytskyy, b. 1970, lodged 19 March 2024, represented by M. Mishalova).

Kulish: his wife was admitted to Kharkiv City Hospital No. 27 on 1 September 2013 with a suspected heart attack; he warned doctors of her severe drug allergies. She died the next day from pulmonary oedema. A criminal investigation into medical negligence began on 21 September 2013. The applicant and his son were questioned in October 2013, and two doctors in January 2014. Medical records sought in 2014 were not provided. A September 2014 forensic examination was refused in March 2015 for lack of a post-mortem report and histological samples. After a court access order of 7 April 2015, the post-mortem report was obtained on 28 April 2015, but the samples were allegedly destroyed. Report No. 217-KE/2015 of 31 July 2015 found no evidence of improper treatment but noted that microscopic assessment was impossible without samples. Proceedings were discontinued on 14 July 2016 without informing the applicant. On 22 November 2019 the Kyivskyy District Court quashed that decision and ordered further investigation, finding no official confirmation that the samples were destroyed. The investigator received the decision on 10 January 2020 but did nothing; in April 2023 the authority said it was unaware of it.

Tsmokalov: his father, diagnosed in January 2018 with colorectal cancer and liver metastases, allegedly complained to his family doctor for about two years without oncology referral. Treatment occurred in 2018–2019; on 17 July 2019 it was discontinued and home care recommended. On 26 July 2019 criminal proceedings opened under Article 140 § 1 after the applicant complained of late diagnosis and inadequate care. The father died on 24 March 2021. A 2020 forensic examination and regional reviews found care compliant. A further examination completed on 17 September 2021 also found no violations; the applicant challenged it. On 16 December 2021 an investigating judge ordered a commission examination by the State Bureau of Forensic Medicine, including COVID-19 treatment questions; it was not performed. On 8 August 2022 the Bureau refused, citing complaints and pressure. A new examination ran from 27 June 2023 to 18 March 2024; opinion no. 54 found timely, protocol-compliant care and no improper treatment. On 11 October 2024 proceedings were terminated for lack of a criminal offence. On 22 August 2025 the Mukachevo City District Court quashed that termination.

Pereta: on 20 April 2017, during a difficult delivery, witnesses said she lost consciousness twice and two doctors, including Dr S., performed the Kristeller manoeuvre. Her baby was born cyanotic, not breathing or swallowing, with an occipital haematoma; after six weeks in intensive care and no development, the child died on 8 January 2018 from pneumonia due to an absent swallowing reflex. She alleged birth trauma and hypoxia from inadequate care, particularly the Kristeller manoeuvre, and lodged a criminal complaint on 6 May 2017. A May 2018 expert commission found care compliant without assessing the Kristeller allegations. Later forensic examinations in November 2018 and June 2019 also found no malpractice and did not address that issue. From 2019–2023 she complained of inactivity; prosecutors acknowledged deficiencies and issued instructions. The limitation period expired on 17 April 2022. Doctors were first questioned only in October 2024–March 2025 and could not recall events. The investigation remains pending.

Broznytskyy: on 24 August 2007 his son was severely injured as a motorbike passenger, admitted to Chemerivtsi District Hospital, and died the following night. On 18 September 2007 a hospital conference found treatment shortcomings; six doctors were reprimanded. A November 2007 forensic examination found death caused by treatment defects. On 3 December 2007 criminal proceedings into medical negligence began. Between 2008 and 2022 examinations confirmed shortcomings and that death could possibly have been prevented. Proceedings were repeatedly terminated and those decisions quashed by prosecutors or courts. In 2022 the prosecutor moved to terminate due to expiry of the statute of limitations; the Khmelnytskyy Court of Appeal terminated the proceedings, upheld by the Supreme Court on 21 November 2023.
001-250309:
The applicant company, OÜ Parem Kallas, based in Pärnu, lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 28 April 2023 concerning the length of domestic proceedings and its impact on compensation for its parcel designated for public use.

In 2000 A.S. bought a riverside plot designated industrial land for EEK 374,800 (approx. EUR 24,000) and sought a detailed plan. On 28 June 2001 Pärnu municipality adopted a plan designating 85% as residential land and about 15% (“the parcel”) as transport land for a future road extension. Under section 30(5) of the Planning and Construction Act, the municipality had to acquire the parcel for a fair price paid promptly upon the owner’s application. On 2 May 2001 A.S. promised not to request acquisition before road works were intended.

In May 2002 A.S. transferred the entire plot to the applicant as a non-monetary contribution; it was valued at EEK 500,000 (approx. EUR 31,955). The applicant requested acquisition in July 2002 and repeated this in 2003 and 2004. In August 2004 it asked a court to order purchase, claiming approx. EUR 60,460. In April 2006 the Tallinn Court of Appeal ordered the municipality to decide within two months, noting the parcel had not been residential land.

On 30 May 2006 the municipality set the price at EUR 6,710 based on a 2004 expert report treating the parcel as transport land. The applicant challenged it but in July 2006 said it would accept that sum as partial payment; in October 2008 it sought default interest. Courts set the decision aside. On 29 May 2012 the Supreme Court stated that the acquisition obligation was unaffected by the ownership change; value depended on the pre-plan industrial designation and referred to 2001; delay damage belonged in separate proceedings.

In July 2012 the municipality offered EUR 37,000 based on an industrial-land report; the applicant refused. Later reports by P. (EUR 92,400) and A. (EUR 12,900) differed. From 2012 to 2017 the municipality set the price four more times; one decision was annulled and two were set aside. A December 2012 decision of EUR 12,900 was set aside on 3 July 2015 (final 8 October 2015). A December 2015 decision of EUR 30,000 based on a K. report was set aside on 12 April 2017 (final 16 November 2017). In July 2015 the applicant proposed EUR 438,099; no compromise resulted. Municipality offers in 2014–2016 ranged from EUR 38,000 to EUR 38,700; the applicant asked EUR 61,000. On 26 June 2017 the municipality decided to acquire for EUR 30,000, reflecting 2001 value. The Tallinn Court of Appeal upheld this on 21 December 2018, noting the K. report was adequate and that an EUR 45,000 offer had been refused; the judgment became final on 14 May 2019.

In 2012 the applicant also began damages proceedings, claiming about EUR 420,000 for inflation, lost investment interest, default interest and maintenance costs. These were suspended from 2014 to 2019 at the applicant’s request. In August 2019 the applicant reduced its claim to about EUR 108,000, retracted some heads, and added a non-pecuniary claim, arguing excessive length affected its economic activity and caused stress to board member A.K. in a criminal case. The Tallinn Administrative Court rejected the non-pecuniary claim on 10 October 2019 and dismissed the pecuniary claim on 13 January 2021 because the sale was not finalised. On appeal, the Tallinn Court of Appeal found on 12 January 2022 that the October 2019 decision had been served and was final, noted the applicant had refrained from concluding the sale, but awarded EUR 16,965 for loss of purchasing power, payable after title transfer. The municipality appealed. The sale was agreed on 18 October 2022 for EUR 30,000. On 28 February 2023 the Supreme Court dismissed the pecuniary claims, finding a delay from 30 May 2006 to July 2012 and that the applicant’s refusal of the July 2012 offer broke the causal link; it denied inflation and other compensation.
001-250316:
The applicant, Ms Ivana Raspović, is a Croatian national born in 1983, living in Sukošan, and working as a lawyer. She represented a client in civil proceedings before the Zadar Municipal Court, presided over by Judge M.P. That court rejected her client’s claim. On 27 June 2019 the applicant lodged an appeal against the judgment, criticising Judge M.P.’s allegedly prolonged inactivity. She stated that the judge was “obviously not feeling like doing his job” and “not reading properly and not seeing the indication [of the defendants] in the statement of claim, which is the problem of the court and not the plaintiff”.

On 9 July 2019 Judge M.P. fined the applicant HRK 3,000 (approximately EUR 400) for contempt of court under section 110 of the Civil Procedure Act, finding that her communication with the court had been inappropriate. The court noted that the statutory fine ranged from HRK 500 to HRK 10,000 and that HRK 3,000 was sufficient in the circumstances.

On 25 July 2019 the applicant appealed against that decision. She emphasised that she had only criticised the judge’s work. She also insisted that the judge was “not doing his job”, “was doing absolutely nothing in [that] court”, and “had abused his authority”. She wrote, preserving capitalisation, that if the judge were doing his job, she would be happy to donate the HRK 3,000 to the State budget if those funds were immediately redistributed as an incentive or bonus to Judge M.P.; even a maximum fine would not change the fact, reality, and truth that the judge did absolutely nothing in that court. She added that Judge M.P. had abused his authority while performing his duties.

On 26 July 2019 the Zadar Municipal Court, through Judge M.P., fined the applicant HRK 10,000 (approximately EUR 1,330) for contempt of court for remarks made in the appeal against the 9 July 2019 decision. The court considered that she had previously been fined for similar conduct but had continued to insult the court and had stated that she would not stop even if given the maximum penalty.

On 6 August 2019 the applicant lodged a supplement to her appeal against the 9 July 2019 ruling, arguing that the sanction was excessive and that she had been expressing strong criticism. On 16 August 2019 she appealed and on 25 November 2019 supplemented her appeal against the 26 July 2019 ruling, reiterating her earlier arguments and stating that even a maximum fine would not change the fact that Judge M.P. was not doing his job.

On 30 January 2020 the Osijek County Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal and upheld the 9 July 2019 ruling. The same day, it varied the 26 July 2019 decision and reduced the fine to HRK 4,000 (approximately EUR 530). On 18 March 2020 the applicant filed a petition for leave to appeal on points of law against both County Court decisions; the Supreme Court declared it inadmissible on 28 July 2020. On 20 March 2020 she lodged a constitutional complaint against both County Court rulings, complaining of a violation of freedom of expression. On 2 June 2021 the Constitutional Court rejected the complaint. It referred to Article 10 case-law principles and held that the interference was not disproportionate to the legitimate aim of maintaining judicial authority and respect for the court. It considered that the language implied the judge was incompetent and was not an appropriate way to object to allegedly excessive length of proceedings, and that the fines had not created a chilling effect on the applicant’s ability to use permissible means to protect her clients’ rights.

On 17 September 2020 the Croatian Bar Association initiated disciplinary proceedings against the applicant for a serious breach of professional duty; according to the latest information from the parties, those proceedings remain pending.

The applicant complained under Article 10 that the fines imposed on her interfered with her freedom of expression, were not based in law, had no legitimate aim, and were not necessary. She alleged that she had criticised the judge’s work without intending to offend him and that the fines had had a chilling effect on her.
001-250415:
Ms Kışanak and Ms Tuncel are well-known Turkish political figures engaged with the “Kurdish question.” Both were elected as independent deputies in 2007 and 2011 and later joined pro-Kurdish parties. Ms Kışanak was co-chair of the BDP from 2011 to 2014 and, at the time of her detention, was mayor of Diyarbakır Metropolitan Municipality. Ms Tuncel held senior positions in pro-Kurdish parties, including HDP co-chair from 2013 to 2014, and was co-chair of the DBP when detained.

The applications concerned the applicants’ pre-trial detention on suspicion of membership of an armed terrorist organisation under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code. They relied on Articles 5, 10, 11 and 18 of the Convention.

On 25 October 2016 Ms Kışanak was arrested at Diyarbakır Airport in a criminal investigation by the Diyarbakır chief public prosecutor’s office into alleged links to the PKK/KCK. On 30 October 2016 the Diyarbakır 1st Magistrate’s Court ordered her pre-trial detention for membership of an armed terrorist organisation. The magistrate relied on, among other things, her participation between 2011 and 2016 in PKK/KCK-requested programmes, demonstrations, rallies, funerals and press events; respectful references to Abdullah Öcalan and descriptions of deceased militants as “martyrs”; use of terms such as “Kurdistan”; involvement in DTK activities; use of municipal resources for funerals with PKK/KCK flags and militant photographs on official vehicles; designation of part of Bağlar cemetery as a “PKK martyrs’ graveyard”; a commemoration in the municipal council building; seized publications; and a CD found at her residence.

On 11 November 2016 the public prosecutor indicted Ms Kışanak for establishing or leading an armed terrorist organisation, disseminating propaganda on 41 counts, participating in unlawful meetings and demonstrations, and failing to disperse from an unlawful gathering. The indictment was accepted on 28 November 2016. On 22 February 2017 the Malatya 1st Assize Court, to which the case had been transferred, extended her detention. It was extended several times until 16 May 2024, and objections were rejected.

On 4 November 2016 Ms Tuncel was arrested at a demonstration outside the Diyarbakır courthouse protesting against arrests of HDP members of parliament and chairpersons. A criminal investigation was opened into her alleged PKK/KCK links. On 6 November 2016 the Diyarbakır 2nd Magistrate’s Court ordered her pre-trial detention for membership of an armed terrorist organisation. The magistrate relied on her participation in DTK meetings, as shown by an anonymous witness and another suspect; speeches between December 2015 and August 2016 allegedly praising the PKK and its leader, describing PKK violence as “resistance,” calling deceased militants “martyrs,” and characterising the “trench events” and attempts to establish autonomous administrations as legitimate resistance; attendance at funerals of deceased militants; and threatening rhetoric against security forces during unlawful demonstrations.

On 22 November 2016 the public prosecutor indicted Ms Tuncel for membership of an armed terrorist organisation and disseminating propaganda. The indictment was accepted on 30 November 2016. On 22 February 2017 the Malatya 1st Assize Court extended her detention. On 21 April 2017 it refused her release request, and on 2 May 2017 the Malatya 2nd Assize Court dismissed her objection. Her detention was extended several times until 16 May 2024.

The cases against both applicants were joined and transferred on 3 February 2017 to the Malatya 1st Assize Court for security reasons. On 1 February 2019 that court convicted Ms Kışanak of membership of an armed terrorist organisation and propaganda, sentencing her to 10 years and 15 months’ imprisonment plus 1 year and 24 months’ imprisonment. It convicted Ms Tuncel of the same offences, sentencing her to 9 years and 9 months’ imprisonment plus 1 year and 24 months’ imprisonment. On 17 July 2019 the Gaziantep Regional Court of Appeal quashed those convictions but ordered that the applicants remain in pre-trial detention. According to publicly available information, both were released on 16 May 2024.

Ms Kışanak lodged individual applications with the Constitutional Court on 5 May and 17 July 2017, complaining of violations of Articles 5, 10 and 18 and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. Ms Tuncel lodged an individual application on 18 May 2017, complaining of violations of Articles 5, 10 and 18. Both applicants lodged applications with the European Court of Human Rights on 12 September 2017.
001-250445:
The applicant, Pero Šarac, born in 1972, lodged application no. 38309/21 against Croatia on 21 July 2021. He was represented by Ms L. Horvat, a lawyer practising in Zagreb. The Croatian Government was given notice of the application.

The domestic background concerns criminal proceedings. On 13 July 2019 the applicant was arrested on drug-trafficking charges. On 14 May 2020 he was indicted, together with seven other persons, for trafficking 600 kilos of cocaine from Central and South America to several European countries, as well as for unlawful possession of weapons. Six of his co-accused pleaded guilty. The indictment against the applicant was confirmed on 12 April 2022, and the case was referred to trial. The criminal proceedings against him were still pending in the supplied record.

Starting on 14 July 2019, the domestic authorities ordered and periodically extended the applicant’s pre-trial detention. Initially, detention was ordered on the risks of collusion and reoffending. After he had been indicted, it was extended solely on the risk of reoffending. The applicant was detained in Zagreb Prison. He was released on 28 December 2021.

Before the Court, the applicant principally complained of the inadequate conditions of his detention. He also raised other complaints under the Convention. The appended table sets out the periods and conditions of his detention in Zagreb Prison.

According to the table, the applicant was held in Zagreb Prison during the following periods: from 14 July 2019 to 6 February 2020, lasting 6 months and 24 days; from 11 to 13 February 2020, lasting 3 days; from 9 to 29 June 2021, lasting 21 days; from 5 to 23 July 2021, lasting 19 days; from 23 July to 7 August 2021, lasting 16 days; from 7 to 26 August 2021, lasting 20 days; from 26 to 29 August 2021, lasting 4 days; and from 29 August to 13 September 2021, lasting 16 days.

The table records the following square metres per inmate for those periods: 3.9–4.88 m²; 3.9–4.88 m²; 2.8 m²; 2.8 m²; 3.2 m²; 2.8 m²; 3.2–3.9 m²; and 2.8 m². For the same periods, the specific grievances listed are inadequate temperature, lack of fresh air, lack of or inadequate hygienic facilities, lack of or insufficient natural light, lack of privacy for toilet, and overcrowding.

Those matters formed the factual basis of the applicant’s complaints before the Court. No other concrete events or domestic decisions are set out in the supplied factual record beyond the criminal proceedings, the detention orders and extensions, the periods and measurements in the appended table, and the applicant’s release.
001-250547:
CASE OF RUSU AND HEDEȘ v. ROMANIA concerns two applications, nos. 38382/19 and 38384/19, lodged on 4 July 2019 by Nechita Rusu and Victoria Hedeș, both Romanian nationals born in 1948 and represented by Eugenia Corina Popa. Both applications concern the review of the applicants’ old-age pension rights several years after their initial assessment by the Cluj Pension Authority, and the consequent demand for retroactive repayment of money mistakenly paid as pension.

In application no. 38382/19 (Rusu), by a decision of 19 December 2012, the Cluj Pension Authority established, based on Law no. 263/2010 and several preceding laws containing the same provisions on qualifying working time for farmers’ pensions, that the applicant had attained retirement age. He began receiving a monthly pension of RON 1,150 (approximately EUR 260). On 19 May 2017, the Cluj Pension Authority issued a new revised decision under Law no. 263/2010, correcting the initial assessment because of an error caused by misapplication of the substantive legal provisions. A period during which the applicant had worked on a collective farm (Cooperativa Agricolă de Producție – CAP) should have been excluded because he had not been an ordinary member but an accountant. His monthly pension was reduced by approximately 30%, and he had to repay the State RON 12,749 (approximately EUR 3,000) mistakenly paid over the previous three years, from 1 June 2014 to 31 May 2017. He challenged the revised decision before the national courts and succeeded at first instance. By a final domestic decision of 14 December 2018, the Cluj Court of Appeal allowed an appeal by the pension authority and ruled in its favour. It did not find any fault on the applicant’s part concerning the mistake made at the time of the initial pension assessment.

In application no. 38384/19 (Hedeș), by a decision of 1 March 2006, the Cluj Pension Authority established, based on Law no. 19/2000 and preceding laws, that the applicant had attained retirement age. She began receiving a monthly pension of RON 1,458 (approximately EUR 320). On 19 May 2017, the Cluj Pension Authority issued a new revised decision under Law no. 263/2010, correcting the initial assessment because of an error caused by misapplication of the substantive legal provisions then applicable. A period during which she had worked on a collective farm (CAP) should have been excluded because she had not been an ordinary member but a chief accountant. Her monthly pension was reduced by RON 410 (approximately EUR 90), and she was required to reimburse the State RON 8,939 (approximately EUR 2,000) mistakenly received over the past three years, from 1 June 2014 to 31 May 2017. She challenged the decision before the national courts and succeeded at first instance. By a final domestic decision of 23 November 2018, the Cluj Court of Appeal reversed the first-instance judgment and ruled in favour of the pension authority. It did not find any fault on the applicant’s part concerning the mistake made at the initial assessment.

On 24 February 2025, in a preliminary ruling, the High Court of Cassation and Justice noted a lack of clarity and precision in the relevant domestic legislation and held that work performed during a period in which a person had an individual employment contract with an agricultural collective farm (CAP) could not be counted as qualifying time for determining pension rights.

Both applicants complained about the reassessment of their individual pension rights several years later and the demand for retroactive payment of large sums received as pension over three years, alleging a breach of their rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.
001-250565:
Jovan Iskrenović, born in 1986 and living in Belgrade, lodged application no. 39427/23 against Serbia on 23 October 2023. He was represented by G. Stanišić. The Government were represented by Z. Jadrijević Mladar.

The case arose during the COVID-19 pandemic. In early March 2020 Serbia introduced restrictive measures; a nationwide state of emergency ran from 15 March to 6 May. Restrictions were later eased, but from mid-June infections rose again. On 7 July 2020 the authorities announced that public gatherings of more than five people would be prohibited from 8 July and that a police curfew in Belgrade was likely from 6 p.m. on 10 July until 5 a.m. on 13 July. Between 7 July and early August 2020 protests took place, especially in Belgrade, with arrests following incidents involving police.

The applicant submitted that on 11 July 2020 at about 7.25 p.m. he was walking on Kralja Aleksandra Boulevard in Belgrade, carrying a backpack with an Anonymous/Guy Fawkes mask on the back of his head. He did not notice police nearby, heard footsteps and someone shout “Stop”, and began to run. Police caught him, forced him to the ground and ordered him to sit. He denied insulting them. After checking his identity card, an officer said he was “clean”. They searched his bag, found two small bottles of water, questioned him about the mask, and took him into custody because of it. Bystanders gathered; he asked them to record, some did, and officers told them to disperse and stop recording. He alleged that an officer with initials M.V. assaulted him inside the police vehicle.

The Government submitted that at about 7.25 p.m. a police patrol was on duty on the same boulevard. As they passed, the applicant directed offensive and insulting remarks about the police at them. He moved away; an officer followed to stop and identify him. When ordered to stop, the applicant turned, then ran. After about 20 metres he stumbled and fell, and the officer arrested him. He was taken to a police station and detained because he had been caught in the act of a minor offence, could not be brought before a court immediately, and there was a reasonable suspicion he might abscond or reoffend.

On 12 July 2020 police initiated minor-offence proceedings under Article 22 of the Public Order Act, alleging insulting public officials. Before the Belgrade Minor Offences Court, the applicant and arresting officer V.S. gave differing accounts. The court conducted a face-to-face confrontation. The applicant requested video footage from a nearby shop’s security cameras, but the court refused, saying the facts had been fully established. It convicted him and sentenced him to 60 days’ imprisonment.

On appeal, the applicant complained that the court had refused, without reasons, to obtain the video footage. On 16 July 2020 the Minor Offences Court of Appeal quashed the judgment because the lower court had failed to reason its refusal, and ordered a retrial.

On 21 August 2020, at the retrial, the arresting officer testified again. The applicant’s lawyer renewed the video request and proposed D.B. as a witness, saying D.B. had responded to a public social-media call and claimed to have been present. The court rejected both requests as unnecessary. It again convicted the applicant and imposed a fine of RSD 120,000 (EUR 1,020), credited detention and prior imprisonment, leaving RSD 115,000 (EUR 980) to pay. On appeal, the applicant complained about lack of reasoning and fair-trial breaches. On 21 September 2020 the Court of Appeal upheld the judgment, reasoning that security footage had no sound and the proposed witness could not have heard the words allegedly spoken.

On 28 October 2020 the applicant was allowed to pay in six instalments. On 4 December 2020 the court revoked that decision for non-payment and initiated enforcement. Only RSD 4,661 was collected. On 3 February 2021 the unpaid fine was replaced with 60 days’ imprisonment. The applicant did not appear; police could not locate him, and an arrest warrant was sought. On 10 October 2022 enforcement was suspended because the absolute statutory limitation period had expired.

On 29 October 2020 the applicant lodged a constitutional appeal, complaining that the judgment rested solely on the arresting officer, that no reasons were given for refusing video footage or D.B.’s testimony, and that the appellate court’s factual assertion about D.B. was arbitrary. He argued the video was sought to show he had not walked past the officers, and the witness to testify about the arrest circumstances. On 23 May 2023 the Constitutional Court rejected the appeal as adequately reasoned and fourth-instance in nature. It was served on 23 June 2023.
001-250735:
CASE OF ÇETİN v. TÜRKİYE (Application no. 35454/19)

The applicant, Emre Çetin, is a Turkish national born in 2002 who lives in Istanbul. He was represented by A. Samsum, a lawyer practising in İzmir. The Government of the Republic of Türkiye were represented by their Agent at the time, Hacı Ali Açıkgül, former Head of the Department of Human Rights of the Ministry of Justice. The applicant lodged the application on 28 May 2019.

The application concerns the applicant’s pre-trial detention on suspicion of having committed an armed robbery. The applicant was 14 years old at the material time. On 2 December 2016, the applicant and his co-accused, M.Ş., were placed in pre-trial detention on charges of armed robbery. In that decision, no mention was made of the applicant’s lawyer’s request for the imposition of child-specific alternative measures.

The applicant was released on 17 October 2017. During the whole period of his pre-trial detention, objections lodged by the applicant against his initial and continued detention were dismissed by the competent courts. When dismissing those objections, the judicial authorities referred in a general manner to the following factors: (i) the strong suspicion that the applicant had committed the offence; (ii) the nature of the offence; (iii) the fact that it was among the “catalogue” offences listed in Article 100 § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure; (iv) the severity of the sentence prescribed by law for the offence concerned; (v) the state of the evidence; (vi) the risk that the applicant would abscond and put pressure on witnesses; and (vii) the finding that alternative measures to detention appeared insufficient.

On 8 February 2017, the applicant lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court. On 20 November 2018, the Constitutional Court declared his application inadmissible. As regards his complaints concerning the length of his pre-trial detention and the alleged lack of relevant and sufficient grounds in the decisions ordering and extending his pre-trial detention, the Constitutional Court stated that it was unable to conclude that the applicant’s detention had been disproportionate and arbitrary, notably in view of the domestic courts’ reasoning. The Constitutional Court’s decision was served on the applicant on 28 November 2018.

Relying on Article 5 § 3 of the Convention, the applicant complained in particular about the length of his pre-trial detention, the lack of relevant and sufficient reasons to justify his pre-trial detention, and the fact that no alternative measures had been taken despite his being a minor.
001-250740:
The case concerns 34 applications against Türkiye. The applicants are Turkish nationals listed in the appended table. The lead applicant, Cemalettin Dönmez (application no. 24039/21), lodged his application on 28 April 2021. The remaining applications, nos. 38590/21 to 5366/23, were lodged between 27 July 2021 and 6 January 2023. The applicants, born between 1961 and 1992, reside in various Turkish provinces, including Kütahya, Düzce, Manisa, Bursa, Afyonkarahisar, Antalya, Konya, Isparta, Samsun, Mersin, Aydın, Bolu, Adana, Denizli, Hatay, Ordu, Amasya, Kastamonu, İzmir, Gaziantep, Ankara and Çorum. Some are represented by lawyers.

The applicants’ convictions were for membership of an armed terrorist organisation described by the Turkish authorities as the “Fetullahist Terror Organisation/Parallel State Structure” (FETÖ/PDY), which the authorities considered to be behind the coup attempt of 15 July 2016. The broader domestic background and context was set out in the earlier Grand Chamber judgment Yüksel Yalçınkaya v. Türkiye. The convictions were based decisively on the applicants’ use of an encrypted messaging application named “ByLock”. The domestic authorities and courts considered that ByLock was designed for the exclusive use of FETÖ/PDY members and that establishing the use of that application was sufficient on its own for conviction under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code for membership of an armed terrorist organisation.

Other evidence against the applicants, where any, consisted mainly of: an admission of using ByLock; decrypted message content confirming use of that application; witness statements attesting to such use; membership of a trade union, association or foundation considered to be affiliated with FETÖ/PDY; account activities at Bank Asya, considered by the authorities to be part of the organisation’s financial structure; possession of pro-FETÖ/PDY publications or audio-visual material; participation in trips considered to have been organised by FETÖ/PDY and records of exit from and entry to Türkiye; donations to FETÖ/PDY-affiliated foundations; participation in demonstrations considered supportive of FETÖ/PDY or in other organisational activities; social media posts in favour of the organisation; residence in FETÖ/PDY student houses or dormitories; use of other messaging applications, such as Kakao Talk or Eagle, to communicate with other members; HTS records indicating communications with others prosecuted for the same offence or other digital evidence suggesting membership; employment by and/or membership of FETÖ/PDY-affiliated institutions, organisations or companies; and witness statements about such employment, membership or other connections to FETÖ/PDY.

For some applicants, the convictions were imposed without waiting for detailed ByLock findings and evaluation reports to be submitted to the case files — reports which potentially included decrypted content of communications over ByLock — on the ground that establishing use of the application sufficed for conviction, irrespective of the nature and content of the communications.

After their convictions, the applicants lodged individual applications with the Constitutional Court. That court summarily dismissed them as inadmissible, relying on its case-law endorsing the Court of Cassation’s landmark judgments on the matter. The applicants then applied to the European Court of Human Rights. The complaints before the Court were brought under Article 6 § 1 and Article 7 of the Convention.
001-250760:
The applicant, Bakur Kiguradze, a Georgian national born in 1955 and living in Tbilisi, is an entrepreneur, a member of the Georgian Academy of Energy and a published author. In 2011, after in camera proceedings, he was convicted of espionage and sentenced to nine years’ imprisonment. On 5 December 2012 Parliament declared him a “political prisoner,” along with others. He was released under an Amnesty Act adopted on 12 January 2013. After he requested reopening, a full retrial was conducted; on 16 July 2018 the 2011 conviction was quashed and he was acquitted of all charges.

In 2020, media outlets reported that several companies and entrepreneurs had donated over GEL 2 million to the ruling Georgian Dream party in the first quarter of that year. The applicant was reported to have donated GEL 50,000 (approximately EUR 14,500). Media outlets and opposition politicians questioned his motives and those of other contributors. In that context, MP I.A., interviewed apparently inside the Parliament building, said that corrupt practices were deterring investment and, regarding Georgian Dream’s attitude towards spies for Russia, stated that not only Kiguradze but other individuals convicted of espionage had been released by Georgian Dream as political prisoners, and that no spies had been revealed since; “these people are the political partners of Georgian Dream.”

On 15 July 2020 the applicant instituted civil proceedings against I.A., Mtavari Arkhi Ltd, TV Pirveli Ltd and RFE/RL’s Georgian service. He sought a declaration that he had been discriminated against, retraction of the allegedly defamatory statement, and non-pecuniary damages. He argued that the defendants had disseminated defamatory content referring to his earlier arrest and conviction for espionage for Russia and his release as a political prisoner, but had failed to mention that he had been fully acquitted in the reopened proceedings.

I.A. asked for discontinuation based on parliamentary immunity under the Constitution and the Freedom of Speech and Expression Act. He submitted that his statement referred to Parliament’s decree declaring certain individuals, including the applicant, political prisoners; because that was a political decision, his statement was a political argument made in the exercise of parliamentary duties, not defamation. The applicant replied that the criminal case had been re-examined in 2018 and all espionage charges dismissed, a fact known to I.A. While accepting that an MP could assess Parliament’s decisions, he maintained that the statement portrayed him as a convicted Russian spy released as a political prisoner and was slanderous.

On 5 October 2021 the Tbilisi City Court discontinued the proceedings against I.A. It found that the statement had been made in the context of political expression and in the exercise of his duties as an MP. It referred to the Constitution, Article 10 of the Convention, the Freedom of Speech and Expression Act, the domestic definition of defamation, Supreme Court practice on distinguishing facts from value judgments, and Parliament’s declaration that the applicant was a political prisoner. It noted that I.A. had been an MP since 2016, that the statement was aired on 19 May 2020, and that section 5 of the Act exempted statements made as part of political debate or in relation to MP duties. It also referred to Parliament decree no. 76 of 5 December 2012, which listed the applicant among political prisoners. Applying Supreme Court guidance, it concluded that the statement contained both statements of fact and value judgments, fell within section 5, and allowed discontinuation.

The applicant lodged an interlocutory appeal, reiterating his arguments. On 24 January 2023 a three-judge panel of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal, sitting as final instance, upheld the lower decision in a 13-page ruling, taking note of his arguments but repeating the lower court’s reasoning. The decision was served on 23 February 2023. The proceedings ended on 15 May 2023 in respect of RFE/RL’s Georgian service; they appear to be ongoing as regards the remaining parties.

Domestic law provided that Article 39 § 3 of the Constitution exempts MPs from liability for views expressed inside or outside Parliament while performing their duties. Section 5 of the Freedom of Speech and Expression Act provides that statements made as part of political debate or in relation to MP duties do not incur defamation liability; the court determines this at a preliminary hearing and may terminate proceedings under Articles 209 and 273 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Termination bars a new claim concerning the same parties, subject and grounds, and is appealable under Article 274. In a decision of 17 May 2023 (no. ას-57-2023), the Civil Chamber of the Supreme Court upheld rejection of an MP’s discontinuation request, finding that the statements went beyond mere political debate and amounted to an accusation of a criminal offence lacking sufficient factual basis. The applicant lodged application no. 25784/23 against Georgia on 23 June 2023, relying on Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention.
001-250890:
A.P., a Polish national born in 1978, lives in Northampton, United Kingdom, in a same-sex relationship with E.K., also Polish. A.P. gave birth to R.P. on 27 November 2014 in London. R.P., born in 2014 and living in Northampton, is also a Polish national. The applicants stated that R.P.’s biological father was a man whom A.P. and E.K. met through an internet sperm-donor matching portal and that he did not wish to take part in the child’s upbringing. R.P.’s original birth certificate named A.P. as mother and E.K. as parent. The applicants’ complaints under Article 8 alone and with Article 14 concerned the refusal of Polish authorities to register the foreign birth certificate.

On 23 January 2015 A.P. applied to the Polish Consulate in London for a Polish passport for R.P. She submitted that the application was not accepted and that she received no written reply. On 1 April 2015 she applied again; the consulate requested a Polish birth certificate. On 7 May 2015 the Polish Consul in London said the passport application had been left unprocessed because no Polish birth certificate had been produced. On 29 July 2015 the Minister of the Interior rejected her complaint as unfounded. On 16 May 2016 the Warsaw Regional Administrative Court rejected the applicants’ complaint as inadmissible in law.

On 28 July 2015 the applicants applied to the Myszków Civil Status Registry to register/transcribe the child’s foreign birth certificate in Poland. On 18 August 2015 the Director refused. The Director stated that the authority did not examine the contents of a foreign certificate, but Polish law did not recognise same-sex parents; registration would be contrary to public policy; under Polish law the mother was the woman who gave birth and the father was a man; and it was impossible to register a certificate showing two women as parents. The decision relied on section 7 of the Private International Law Act 2011. The applicants appealed, relying on Article 8, the child’s best interests and the child’s uncertain legal situation.

On 9 October 2015 the Śląski Governor upheld the refusal. The Governor found that transcription could be refused if it contravened fundamental rules of Polish legal order; the foreign certificate was contrary to the Family and Custody Code; Polish law did not allow same-sex unions or adoption by same-sex couples; and the foreign certificate could still be used in Polish courts under Article 1138 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The first applicant appealed, alleging breach of the Constitution and discrimination against the child as a child in a same-sex family. On 6 April 2016 the Gliwice Regional Administrative Court dismissed the appeal. It reasoned that registration would require a woman’s data to be entered in the “father” field, which was not possible; there was no registration of same-sex relationships or second-parent adoption for same-sex parents; and the public policy exception applied. It also stated that transcription was unnecessary because the child could rely on the foreign birth certificate before Polish authorities.

The first applicant lodged a cassation appeal, arguing that a Polish birth certificate was necessary to obtain a Polish passport, relying on the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and the child’s best interests, and alleging discrimination based on the parents’ sexual orientation. On 18 June 2018 the Polish Human Rights Commissioner intervened, observing that under section 104(5) of the 2014 Law on Civil Status Records registration was required for a Polish identity document or PESEL number; that the child’s best interests had not been considered; and that the public policy clause had been applied automatically. On 20 June 2018 the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the cassation appeal, holding that transcription would contravene the domestic legal order and that the child’s best interests were protected by the evidential value of the foreign document under Article 1138 CCP and the Supreme Court’s resolution of 20 November 2012 (III CZP 58/12).
001-251007:
The applicant, Ivan Lazić, a Croatian national born in 1941, lives in Zagreb. He has been disabled since losing both legs in 1959. He practised shooting from 1969, won medals, led the national shooting team for disabled athletes in 1992, 2000 and 2004, and presided over a local shooting club. He owned three pistols, which he kept at the premises of that shooting club. The application was lodged with the European Court on 29 July 2021 by Mr Lazić, represented by Mr M. Čaržavec. The Croatian Government was represented by Ms Š. Stažnik.

In October 2015, minor-offence proceedings were instituted against the applicant on charges of not allowing, on one occasion, the police to verify the conditions for the safekeeping of his three pistols. On 1 December 2015 the Zagreb Minor Offences Court convicted him of the minor offence under section 92 § 1 (4) of the Weapons Act. It also imposed a protective measure under section 92 § 2 of that Act, confiscating his three pistols.

Following an appeal by the applicant, on 4 July 2019 the High Minor Offences Court acquitted him because the new weapons law no longer penalised the behaviour for which he had been charged. That court also quashed the confiscation decision and instructed the first-instance court to examine whether the three pistols should be confiscated under section 76.a of the Minor Offences Act, having regard to the applicant’s personal situation and all other circumstances of the case.

In the remitted proceedings, the Zagreb Minor Offences Court asked the police to carry out a background check to determine the risk of the applicant misusing the pistols. On 20 January 2020 the police reported that the applicant was a retired shooting instructor and member of a hunting association who lived with his wife. He had not displayed signs of illness or problems with gambling or alcohol. His neighbours reported that he lived a peaceful life and was a respected person in the community. The police also reported that the applicant had been convicted in 2017 for sexually abusing a child and that every three months he had to report to a probationary officer.

On 17 April 2020 the Zagreb Minor Offences Court issued a decision confiscating the applicant’s three pistols. The court noted that in 2017 the applicant had been convicted of sexually abusing a child and held that the pistols should be confiscated for the protection of public safety and on moral grounds, in accordance with section 76.a of the Minor Offences Act.

On 27 May 2020 the High Minor Offences Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal. It agreed with the first-instance court that, in the light of the applicant’s 2017 conviction, confiscating the pistols was necessary for the protection of public safety and on moral grounds, and that the requirements for confiscation under section 76.a §§ 1 and 2 of the Minor Offences Act had been met.

By a decision of 24 February 2021, the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s constitutional complaint as unfounded.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the arbitrariness of the domestic courts’ decision to confiscate his pistols. He argued that the confiscation was unlawful because the pistols had not been used to commit the minor offence for which he had been acquitted, and because the criminal conviction on which the domestic courts had based the confiscation had nothing to do with the minor offence in question. He further complained that the domestic courts had entirely failed to take into account that shooting constituted an important aspect of his life and that he used the confiscated pistols to make a living.
001-251023:
The case concerns two applications lodged against North Macedonia by Mr Jovanov, a Macedonian citizen born in 1968 who lives in Skopje and was represented by lawyer A. Godjo. The applications were lodged on 9 June 2020 and 7 August 2020. The applicant alleged that the domestic courts had given insufficient reasons for extending his house arrest in criminal proceedings against him for abuse of office, and that the Skopje Court of Appeal had not reviewed the extension decisions speedily. His complaints were directed at the period from 25 September 2019 until 7 August 2020.

On 27 June 2019 a public prosecutor opened an investigation into abuse of office in respect of the applicant, described as a manager of a private company and a former government official, in the context of criminal proceedings also referred to in Janakieski v. North Macedonia (nos. 57325/19 and 16291/20, 14 November 2023). The prosecutor requested that the applicant be detained in prison. On 28 June 2019 a pre-trial judge ordered his detention in a prison facility. That detention was twice extended. On 3 September 2019 a pre-trial judge of the Skopje Criminal Court of First Instance replaced the detention with house arrest and ordered that the applicant’s passport be seized.

The applicant’s house arrest was subsequently extended three times by a three-judge panel of the appellate court. Those extensions were based on the grounds that he might abscond or interfere with the investigation. After the applicant was indicted on 12 December 2019, his house arrest was extended by a three-judge panel of the trial court eight times within the relevant period, including by decisions of 12 December 2019 and 10 January, 10 February, 11 March, 7 April, 7 May, and 9 June 2020. Those decisions relied solely on the risk that he might abscond. In them, the panel referred to the stage of the proceedings, the type, character and nature of the offence, the degree of criminal liability, the type and severity of the prescribed sentence, and the possibility that a prison sentence might be imposed.

On 23 December 2019 the Supreme Court amended an extension order concerning the applicant’s house arrest from 25 November until 25 December 2019. It found that the house arrest was justified by the risk of his absconding and that he might use connections made as a former government official and a manager of a private company to flee.

The applicant appealed against all extension orders. The appellate court took between 18 and 39 days to decide the appeals against the extension orders mentioned above. In addition to the reasons already set out in the extension orders, some of the appellate court’s decisions also referred to the “high degree of unlawfulness” of the actions for which the applicant was accused and to the pecuniary damage which the offence had allegedly caused to the budget as reasons justifying the risk that he might abscond.

On 27 August 2020 the applicant’s house arrest was replaced with a prohibition on leaving his place of residence, an obligation to report weekly to the court, temporary seizure of his passport, a prohibition on being issued a new passport, and a prohibition on crossing State borders with an identity card.
001-251024:
The applicants are Rainbow Mission Foundation, a Hungarian NGO promoting LGBTQI equality, and four Hungarian nationals: Sándor Jámbor, Ákos Ányos Hadházy, Bernadett Szél and Gergely István Gazda. They complained under Articles 10 and 11 that measures taken during Hungary’s COVID-19 bans on public gatherings in 2020–2021 were unnecessary and disproportionate.

Hungary registered its first COVID-19 infection on 4 March 2020; the WHO declared a pandemic on 11 March. The Government declared a state of danger on 11 March 2020 by Decree no. 40/2020. Decree no. 46/2020 of 16 March 2020 prohibited public gatherings and remained in force until 17 June 2020. On 3 November 2020 the Government declared a second state of danger with effect from 4 November. Decree no. 484/2020 of 10 November imposed a curfew and prohibited all events and gatherings except religious ceremonies; public gatherings were banned until 22 May 2021. Sections 4(1) and 5(1)–(2) prohibited gathering or being present at a gathering, with limited exceptions. The Right of Assembly Act required prior notification to the police at least 48 hours before an announced gathering.

The applicant association notified the police on 5 December 2020 of a planned demonstration near Parliament on 10 December 2020 against legislative amendments affecting LGBTQI persons. Up to 30 participants would sit in cars in a closed area, wearing masks, keeping distance, displaying banners and sounding horns. At a 6 December consultation, police stated that Decree no. 484/2020 prohibited the event and that notification would necessarily lead to a ban. On 7 December the police prohibited the demonstration because of the general ban, without examining health risks. On 15 December the Kúria rejected the association’s request to set aside the decision and refer the case to the Constitutional Court, finding the ban lawful and the general prohibition precluding consideration of individual circumstances. On 22 June 2021 the Constitutional Court rejected the association’s constitutional complaint against sections 4(1), 5(1) and 5(2).

The first applicant, a retired police officer in Gyula, notified police on 21 March 2021 of a planned 26 March demonstration. Ten participants were expected in separate cars, wearing masks, driving, sounding horns and using loudspeakers to criticise the Government’s pandemic handling. After a 22 March consultation, police prohibited the event on 23 March. On 30 March the Kúria rejected his request to set aside the decision, finding it lawful. On 12 July 2021 the Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint, referring to its earlier decision.

The second applicant, an opposition politician, together with the third applicant and Momentum Mozgalom, announced on Facebook weekly gatherings at Clark Ádám Square in Budapest between 20 April and 18 May 2020. These were contact-free car protests using horns to criticise the Government’s pandemic response and demand testing, support for small businesses and transparent information. No police notification was made. He was fined HUF 80,000 on 11 August 2020 for the 20 April event; HUF 100,000 on 25 August for 27 April; and HUF 250,000 on 4 September for 4, 11 and 18 May, also concerning traffic rules and Decree no. 46/2020. Domestic courts later upheld, reduced or terminated parts of those decisions. His constitutional complaint was dismissed on 25 January 2022.

The third applicant participated in the 27 April “Honk so Orbán can hear it!” event, held a press conference and drove around the roundabout sounding her horn; she also attended the 4, 11 and 18 May gatherings. On 9 October 2020 she was fined HUF 250,000 for a minor traffic violation, infringement of Decree no. 46/2020 and abuse of the right of assembly. On 3 March 2021 the District Court terminated the decree-related part, upheld the traffic and assembly findings on four counts and reduced the fine to HUF 100,000. Her constitutional complaint was dismissed on 25 January 2022.

The fourth applicant joined the 11 May 2020 gathering. At 5.05 p.m. he drove around Clark Ádám Square sounding his horn and displaying a banner reading “Solidarity, humane crisis management.” On 19 August 2020 he was fined HUF 150,000 for a minor traffic violation and breach of state-of-danger rules. On 29 January 2021 the District Court terminated the state-of-danger part and issued a warning for the traffic violation. His constitutional complaint was dismissed on 25 January 2022.
001-251025:
The applicant, Mitja Kunstelj, a Slovenian national born in 1970, lives in Ljubljana. He lodged application no. 5257/22 against Slovenia on 19 January 2022. The case concerns criminal proceedings in which he was convicted of insult and slander and sentenced to six months’ imprisonment; the application raised an issue under Article 10. The private prosecutors were two journalists, V.V. and Š.P.

From 2010 the applicant wrote numerous posts on his personal blog about V.V. and Š.P. He insulted V.V. with terms such as “fag”, “homo”, “rat”, “pus-filled sore”, “pervert”, “drunkard”, “cheat”, “scumbag” and “zoophile”, and alleged that V.V. had forced him into a sexual encounter, groped him and abused dogs. He described Š.P. as “that whore from Zalog”, “a real Mata Hari”, “less than a piece of shit”, a “media whore”, a “hussy” and a “prostitute”.

V.V. and Š.P. initiated civil proceedings. On 8 August 2012 the Ljubljana District Court, in civil proceedings, prohibited the applicant from further reporting on V.V. in a manner characterising him as a cheater, liar, sexual harasser or animal abuser, and from using foul language such as “fag”, “homo” and “pus-filled sore”. Over the years courts issued interim injunctions ordering him to stop insulting V.V. and Š.P. through blog posts. He continued, and was fined EUR 10,000 twice for non-compliance. In a later blog post, he threatened V.V. and his counsel with physical violence, which became the subject of separate criminal proceedings.

It also found risks of absconding, aggravated by the severity of punishment faced, influencing witnesses or otherwise interfering with the investigation, and reoffending. The court considered their personal circumstances but concluded that no other preventive measure would suffice. The complaint concerns the Dutch authorities’ refusal of residence permits for five minor children of the applicant, A.A., a Yemeni national born in 1970 and living in Helvoirt. He had contracted polygamous marriages in Yemen with three women and had thirteen children: eight with his first wife, three with his second, and two with his third.

On 17 October 2018 the applicant entered the Netherlands and applied for a temporary asylum residence permit. It was granted on 12 July 2019, valid from 23 October 2018 to 23 October 2023. On 20 November 2023 he received a permanent asylum residence permit valid from 23 October 2023.

On 25 July 2019, while his family members were in Türkiye, the applicant applied for family reunification for his first wife and all thirteen children. On 30 August 2019 the Immigration and Naturalisation Service (IND) informed him that polygamy was contrary to Dutch public order and asked him to choose one marriage for recognition under Dutch law; only that wife and her children would be eligible. On 16 September 2019 the applicant said he wished to maintain the application for his first wife and the children from all three marriages. The authorities treated this as his having chosen the first marriage.

On 27 December 2019 the IND granted reunification for the first wife and their eight children, but refused it for the five children born of the second and third marriages (R., Ra., W., N. and A.). It relied on Article 4(4) of the Family Reunification Directive, as implemented in section 3.16 of the Aliens Decree 2000, which contains a polygamy exception.

On 21 January 2020 the applicant objected, submitting grounds on 21 February 2020. He argued that polygamy was not automatically contrary to public order and that an individual assessment was required. He cited severe consequences of divorce for his second and third wives, including social stigma and discrimination; his children’s disadvantaged situation in Türkiye with temporary kimlik documents and limited access to services; and the impossibility of returning to Yemen because of a real risk of ill-treatment linked to his and the mothers’ human-rights activities. The IND asked on 10 June 2020 whether divorce was possible. In replies of 1 and 30 July 2020, the applicant said he could not contact the Yemeni authorities and that divorce would harm his wives. A hearing was conducted in writing because of COVID-19. He later submitted evidence of financial support, threats, mothers’ declarations consenting to the children living with him, and translations of further threat evidence.

On 21 January 2021 the IND rejected the objection as manifestly ill-founded and maintained the refusal. It considered that the applicant was bound by one recognised marriage; only one wife and her minor children were eligible. It stressed that polygamy was contrary to Dutch public order. It found the children were not in dire circumstances in Türkiye because they lived with their biological mothers, had kimlik documents, and had access to services, housing, schools and private clinics. It noted the applicant had not cared for them since leaving Yemen, could maintain contact and visit them, and had visited in March 2020. It found no compelling interests.

On 19 March 2021 the applicant sought judicial review. He argued he sought reunification only with the children, with the mothers’ consent, not with the second and third wives; that polygamy was not automatically contrary to public order; that divorce and Yemen-related risks should be considered; and that insufficient weight was given to the children’s interests. He submitted a 28 May 2019 psychometric report for R.

On 21 September 2021 the District Court of The Hague, sitting in Amsterdam, declared the review unfounded. It found the IND had wrongly called the objection manifestly ill-founded but treated this as a clerical error. It held that denial was in principle authorised but required an individualised assessment; that asylum-related risks belonged to asylum proceedings; that the children were not in dire circumstances; and that the psychometric report was insufficient.

On 19 October 2021 the applicant appealed to the Administrative Jurisdiction Division, supplementing his appeal on 25 November 2021 and 2 February 2022. He added arguments about changing Dutch views on family structures and polyamory, asylum-related family problems, and the children’s best interests. On 13 October 2022 the Division upheld the dismissal. It reasoned that polygamy was contrary to Dutch public order and public morality, that changing views did not alter this, and that the State Secretary had made an individualised assessment and could attach great weight to the polygamous situation. The rejection became final. Later, the second wife was granted asylum on 24 June 2025, and on 18 July 2025 she applied for family reunification for her children; that application was pending.

The applicant, Pertch Margaryan, an Armenian national born in 1963, lives in Gyumri. His son, A. Margaryan, was conscripted in December 2013 and assigned to military unit no. 38636 of the Nagorno-Karabakh armed forces in Shushi.
