The case involves two applications against Serbia lodged by Serbian nationals. Application no. 34317/17 was brought by Milan Đorđević, born in 1970, residing in Odžaci, represented by Branislav Milojičić, and lodged on 13 April 2017. Application no. 75858/17 was brought by Saša Milosavljević, born in 1965, residing in Pančevo, represented by Branislav Manić, and lodged on 20 October 2017. The Serbian Government was represented by its Agent, Z. Jadrijević Mladar.

The subject matter concerns divergent domestic case-law on dismissal of police officers’ compensation claims for unpaid salary supplements for work on public holidays, night work and overtime (“work during unsociable hours”). From June 2013 onward, domestic courts both upheld and dismissed claims lodged by many colleagues of the applicants. Courts interpreted Article 147 §§ 1 and 3 of the Police Act differently and selected different comparator employees when assessing whether the claimants’ salary coefficients had been increased for work during unsociable hours. This led to conflicting decisions in factually identical claims. On 10 November 2015, seeking to harmonise lower-court case-law, the Supreme Court adopted a guiding legal opinion. It stated that a “comparable worker” had to be an authorised officer, rather than a civilian officer, with the same level of education as the claimant but who did not work during unsociable hours. Applying that method, lower courts subsequently allowed similar claims. Where courts continued to rule contrary to the legal opinion, the Supreme Court quashed the decisions and ordered retrials, or reversed appellate decisions following appeals on points of law.

As regards the applicants, on 20 April and 10 September 2015 the competent first-instance courts dismissed their claims, comparing their salary coefficients with those of civilian officers who had not worked during unsociable hours. The competent courts of appeal upheld those decisions, which became final on 4 and 16 December 2015. The applicants lodged constitutional appeals against those decisions, complaining of case-law divergence and noting that certain courts had allowed identical claims brought by their colleagues. The first applicant submitted evidence of inconsistent case-law in which courts had ruled in favour of claimants by comparing their salary coefficients with those of authorised officers. The applicants also complained that the lower courts had applied substantive law arbitrarily.

On 8 December 2016 the Constitutional Court dismissed the first applicant’s constitutional appeal. Referring to its previous decision no. Už-3827/2012 of 12 December 2012, it held that he had relied on a comparison with cases in which compensation claims had been upheld on different grounds, rather than on a differing method of comparison of salary coefficients. On 20 September 2017 the Constitutional Court dismissed the second applicant’s constitutional appeal as unsubstantiated, because he had relied only on two first-instance decisions and had not demonstrated that those decisions had become final.

The applicants are three Moldovan nationals, Galina Roşca and others. On 14 March 2015 they lodged an application alleging a breach of the principle of legal certainty and complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

R.P. had four children: R.I., R.T., R.G. and R.Gr. R.P. died in April 2000. By will, he left plots of land (“the testate property”) to R.I. Within six months of R.P.’s death, R.I. formally accepted the succession under the will and on 8 November 2000 received a certificate as heir to the testate property. The first applicant had been married to R.G. until his death before R.P.’s death. The second and third applicants are their children. Before R.P. died, the applicants lived on his property and continued to live there afterwards.

In February 2011 R.I., represented by G.A., obtained from the notary handling R.P.’s succession a certificate attesting his right to part of the property not covered by the will. He donated that property to G.V. On 29 March 2011 G.V. brought court proceedings seeking the applicants’ removal from the disputed property. On 30 March 2011 the applicants counterclaimed, seeking annulment of the certificate recognising R.I. as heir to the intestate part and of the donation to G.V., and recognition that they had de facto accepted R.P.’s succession by living on the property.

On 15 November 2011 the Criuleni District Court accepted G.V.’s claims and rejected the applicants’ claims. It found that R.I. had accepted the succession within six months and that, because R.G. was already dead when R.P. died, the applicants had no right to the property as R.G.’s heirs by law.

On 15 May 2012 the Chișinău Court of Appeal overturned that judgment and accepted the applicants’ claims. It found that the applicants had taken the rank R.G. would have had if alive when R.P. died. They had de facto accepted the succession by living on the property. It also found that none of R.P.’s other children, including R.I., had accepted the succession of the property not covered by the will within six months. R.I. had missed the six-month deadline and, when he acted in February 2011, had done so through a representative, G.A., contrary to law. The court found that R.I. “did not have the legal or moral right to [the disputed property]”.

R.I. and G.V. appealed on points of law. They argued that R.I.’s acceptance within six months covered the entire property he could inherit, both the testate property and his share of the remainder. They said the Court of Appeal had ignored R.I.’s formal acceptance and that, under the applicable law, accepting a succession covered the whole estate.

On 2 January 2013 the Supreme Court of Justice upheld the lower judgment. It found that in 2000 R.I. had requested only a certificate based on the will, not one for intestate inheritance, which he requested in 2011. On 30 April 2014 the same court rejected an extraordinary appeal by R.Gr., who complained that he had not been involved in the proceedings and that the higher courts had not reacted to notarised declarations by two of R.P.’s nieces and nephews, including applicant Ms Roșca Diana, stating that they refused to inherit R.P.’s property.

On 27 May 2013 the applicants brought a second set of proceedings against the notary, asking to annul the certificate attesting that Roșca Andrei, the second applicant, was heir to one quarter of the intestate part, and to replace it with certificates giving each of the three applicants one third of that property. On 11 December 2013 the Criuleni District Court accepted their claims, finding that facts established in a final court decision did not have to be proved again and could not be contested in later proceedings. On 30 July 2014 the Chișinău Court of Appeal set that decision aside and rejected the claims. It found that the 15 May 2012 judgment, although final, had only established the applicants’ right to inherit, not that they were the only heirs. Since R.I. had also accepted the succession within six months, he had the right to obtain part of the property not covered by the will. The applicants appealed, arguing that the Court of Appeal had not properly considered the 15 May 2012 judgment, which had established that R.I. had no right to the disputed property. On 3 December 2014 the Supreme Court rejected the appeal as unfounded.

M.C., a Serbian national born in 1978 who lived in Jászapáti, had resided in Hungary since 2010 for employment purposes. On 22 February 2022 he lodged a request for a residence permit for employment. On 25 April 2022 the National Directorate-General for Aliens Policing (NDGAP) dismissed the application, relying on an opinion from the Jász-Nagykun-Szolnok police department that his residence posed a threat to public safety. He appealed. On 7 July 2022 the NDGAP at second instance quashed the first-instance decision, finding, on the basis of a police opinion obtained in the appeal, that he did not constitute a risk, and remitted the case.

On 13 October 2022, in the resumed proceedings, the NDGAP dismissed the application and expelled him to Serbia. It held that the conditions for a residence permit concerning employment, housing, sufficient means and health insurance were met. However, the Constitution Protection Office (CPO), in an opinion of 27 September 2022, established that he posed a threat to national security. The NDGAP therefore dismissed the request under sections 13(1)(h) and 18(1)(a) of Act no. II of 2007 on the admission and right of residence of third-country nationals. The underlying information in the CPO assessment was classified under Act no. CLV of 2009 on the protection of classified information.

The applicant appealed. In the appeal proceedings, the CPO maintained its findings concerning the national security risk. Relying on that assessment, the NDGAP at second instance emphasised that, given the CPO’s opinion, consideration of any other conditions was excluded.

The applicant sought judicial review. On 5 April 2023 the Debrecen High Court dismissed his action. It held that the NDGAP was not bound by the CPO’s assessment, but, in the absence of any circumstances suggesting otherwise, it based its decision exclusively on that assessment. It explained that there was no opportunity to consider the applicant’s personal circumstances, since the existence of a national security risk made rejection of the residence permit compulsory. Such risk had been established by the CPO. The trial judge consulted the classified documents and confirmed the CPO’s assessment. On 20 June 2023 the Kúria declared the applicant’s petition for judicial review inadmissible. The applicant did not lodge a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court.

Meanwhile, the applicant requested access to the CPO’s classified report under the Classified Information Act. On 11 November 2022 the CPO rejected his application. His request for judicial review of that rejection was to no avail.

In unrelated constitutional complaint cases, the Constitutional Court found that whether an individual’s presence in Hungary constituted a threat to national security could not be reassessed in constitutional proceedings, as that would amount to re-examination of the facts; that task belonged to ordinary courts. It also held that it could not review access to classified information and related procedural questions where those had not been subject to the immigration proceedings concerned by the constitutional complaint.

The applicant complained under Article 8 that, for want of any connection with his country of origin, his expulsion violated his right to respect for his private life. He further complained that he had been expelled without sufficient procedural guarantees. Relying on Article 13, he submitted that, without access to the grounds of the alleged national security risk, he had had no effective remedy against the expulsion decision.

Anar Mammadov, an Azerbaijani national born in 1979 and living in Baku, is a journalist and chief editor of the news website criminal.az. He had been formally warned by prosecuting authorities in 2015 and 2017 over articles alleged to contain false and biased information. On 3 July 2018 an assassination attempt was made on E.V., head of the Ganja City Executive Authority, leaving him and his bodyguard seriously injured. Riots followed in Ganja, during which two police officers were killed. Between 3 and 5 July 2018 the applicant published articles discussing possible causes of the attack. Two articles later formed the basis of charges against him.

On 9 July 2018 the Prosecutor General’s Office stated that certain media had spread false and provocative information about a “premeditated act of terror,” inciting terrorism, forcible seizure of power and constitutional change. Criminal proceedings were instituted under Articles 214-2 and 281.1 of the Criminal Code, and also under Article 313 regarding criminal.az and other websites. The same day the applicant was questioned by the Baku City Prosecutor’s Office for several hours without a lawyer. He claimed investigators seized and examined his two mobile telephones without a court order. He was required to sign a dictated statement consenting to hand over two mobile telephones, two laptops and criminal.az-related documents for the Article 313 investigation. An investigator then issued a seizure decision relying on Article 243.3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The seizure was carried out at the applicant’s flat in his presence and before two attesting witnesses. A laptop and Criminal.az LLC documents were seized; a laptop belonging to his wife was inspected. No court order was provided. A seizure record stated the handover was voluntary; the applicant signed it but later said he was not given a copy. On 11 July 2018 he appealed to the Baku Court of Appeal against presumed court authorisations by the Sabail and Sabunchu District Courts. The Sabunchu District Court had issued no such decision, and his appeal was returned. On 18 July he asked the Prosecutor General’s Office to return the items and clarify his procedural status. On 24 August the office replied that he had been questioned initially without representation and later with a representative, and that a lawful decision on the items would be issued. On 23 July he complained to the Sabail District Court under Article 449 of the Code of Criminal Procedure; on 26 July that court refused to hear it, and on 27 August the Baku Court of Appeal upheld that refusal. On 6 December 2018 the seized laptop was recognised as physical evidence; the telephones were to be returned, but the laptop was retained. The applicant claimed the items were returned five years later in unusable condition.

In the criminal proceedings, a forensic linguistic examination was ordered on 10 July 2018. On 31 October 2018 the expert reported that the articles contained public calls against the State, including incitement to hatred, unrest and disobedience. On 12 December 2018 the applicant was charged under Articles 281.2, 309.2 and 313. On 18 March 2019 the Baku Court of Serious Crimes convicted him on all counts, sentencing him to five years and six months’ imprisonment suspended for two years, plus a two-year ban on public office. It relied on the expert report and statements from two Baku women who said they felt anxious and frightened after reading the articles. The applicant appealed, arguing the proceedings were fabricated and interfered with his private and professional life; the articles concerned public interest, quoted other media and contained value judgments. On 4 June 2019 the Baku Court of Appeal upheld the conviction. On 25 February 2020 the Supreme Court partially upheld the convictions under Articles 281.2 and 313, reclassified Article 309.2 to 309.1, and reduced the sentence to five years and three months suspended for two years, with the same public-office ban.

Ms Müyesser Uğur, born in 1963 and living in Ankara, is a journalist who has written on Turkish military-political relations, domestic politics and national security. At the relevant time she published on the website odatv.com about a military cooperation agreement between the Turkish Government and the Libyan Government of National Accord and the deployment of Turkish Armed Forces to Libya. The articles cited in the investigation were published on 19 December 2019 (“What kind of ‘soldiers’ will be sent to Libya?”), 24 December 2019 (“Who are these Turkish commanders who met with Haftar?”), 20 January 2020 (“Which commander went to Libya? Who replaced him?”), and 23 February 2020 (“When, how and in what capacity did the Syrian National Army go to Libya”). Two further articles dated 23 May 2018 and 25 November 2019 were also included later.

On 13 November 2019 the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office received a tip-off that E.B., a sergeant at Hadımköy Military Barracks, was leaking confidential military information. On 3 December 2019 the Ankara 4th Magistrate’s Court ordered the wiretapping of E.B.’s phone. Calls between E.B. and the applicant were intercepted, mainly concerning Turkish military operations in Libya and Syria. On 9 January 2020 the Ankara 7th Magistrate’s Court ordered wiretapping of the applicant’s phone. In a call on 13 January 2020 the applicant asked E.B. who the high-level commander sent to Libya would be; E.B. said it was M.G., then Deputy Chief of the General Staff. On 15 April 2020 access to the investigation file was restricted. On 8 June 2020 E.B. and the applicant were arrested and the applicant’s home was searched.

On 11 June 2020 police and the public prosecutor questioned the applicant about her phone communications with E.B. and her articles. She denied obtaining or publishing State secrets, said her articles relied on publicly available information, and stated that E.B. had only spoken to her by phone and had sent no documents. The police report alleged that six articles contained confidential information obtained from E.B. The public prosecutor requested pre-trial detention under Article 329 of the Criminal Code for disclosing information relating to State security and political interests. The Ankara 3rd Magistrate’s Court ordered the applicant’s detention the same day, finding strong suspicion, risk of tampering with evidence and absconding. Her appeal was dismissed on 23 June 2020, and detention was extended several times.

The Ministry of National Defence confirmed that the information that Lieutenant General M.G. had gone to Libya as commander was accurate and that related documents were classified “Confidential (1), Confidential (2).” On 23 September 2020 the public prosecutor issued a bill of indictment referring to six articles. The Ankara 26th Assize Court accepted it on 29 September 2020. On 9 November 2020 the applicant was released subject to judicial control. On 11 December 2020 a further indictment charged her with obtaining State security information under Article 327; the cases were joined. On 8 March 2021 the Assize Court convicted her of obtaining prohibited information under Article 334 (one year and ten days) and disclosing prohibited information under Article 336 (two years and six months), suspending only the first sentence. It found that only the 20 January 2020 article contained significant State-interest information, acquitted her under Articles 327 and 329, and ordered her immediate detention upon conviction.

On 3 November 2022 the Ankara Court of Appeals upheld the convictions with final effect; the acquittals remained subject to appeal before the Court of Cassation. As of 2 April 2024 the criminal proceedings were still pending before the Court of Cassation.

On 3 July 2020 the applicant lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court. On 7 April 2022 the Plenary Constitutional Court found no breach of her constitutional rights to liberty and security or freedom of expression. It examined the detention in light of both Articles 329 and 327, found reasonable suspicion as to the 20 January 2020 article, and considered the disclosed commander information capable of causing potential danger. Four judges dissented, arguing that suspicion should have been assessed only under Article 329, that the commander’s rank had already been publicly disclosed, that no clear lawful prohibition or harm had been shown, and that detention was not necessary or proportionate.

The applicant, Norbert Kostov, a Slovak national born in 1978, was detained in Budapest. A criminal investigation into a double homicide committed by Slovak nationals began after human remains were found in Hungary on 9 July 2018; they had apparently been hidden there in February 2016. In February 2019 the Hungarian and Slovak authorities set up a joint investigation team. On 20 July 2020 the Buda Central District Court issued a European Arrest Warrant. The applicant was arrested in Slovakia on 24 July 2020 and handed over to Hungary. The same day he was heard as a suspect for homicide against multiple persons with premeditation and for gain.

On 26 July 2020 the investigating judge remanded him in detention. The grounds were a reasonable suspicion, flight risk due to a possible life sentence, risk of tampering with evidence, and risk of reoffending based on previous Hungarian and Slovak convictions. Criminal supervision was considered insufficient. Appeals were dismissed. From August 2020 to April 2022 the District Court repeatedly extended detention. Reasons included flight, obstruction, reoffending, untraced proceeds allegedly worth hundreds of thousands of euros, ongoing investigation, threats to kill a witness reported in December 2021, a later-discontinued investigation for preparation of homicide, and expert psychological findings describing him as antisocial, aggressive, manipulative and inclined to criminal behaviour. In January 2021 the defence offered declarations and a surety of 20 million Hungarian forints (about EUR 55,000); the High Court rejected these as not mitigating flight risk without certified information about the relatives’ material circumstances.

In February 2022 the District Court found that the risk of obstructing proceedings had ended because the investigation was complete, but continued detention based on flight and reoffending risks. On 2 March 2022 the High Court upheld that decision, finding no obstruction risk but flight and reoffending risks, and that no less restrictive measure would suffice.

On 22 May 2022 the prosecution indicted the applicant and two others for homicide as joint offenders, two counts of grievous bodily harm, and attempted vandalism. The investigation file exceeded 20,000 pages. On 22 June 2022 the Budapest High Court, as trial judge, extended detention until first-instance judgment, citing flight and reoffending; the Budapest Court of Appeal upheld this on 19 July 2022. Hearings took place in October and December 2022. Further reviews occurred on 16 December 2022, upheld on 2 February 2023; then on 18 July 2023, 12 February 2024 and 1 October 2024. The Court of Appeal relied on the gravity of charges, possible life sentence, lack of personal or business attachments in Hungary, criminal connections abroad, criminal history, and expert evidence. In October 2024 it addressed the passage of more than four years since first remand and held that the reasons for detention had neither become less pressing nor ceased, and that the public interest outweighed the applicant’s personal freedom. The Kúria upheld the February 2024 decision on 10 April 2024. The High Court held fifteen hearings in 2023, fifteen in 2024 and six in 2025. On 2 April 2025 it convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to life imprisonment with no possibility of parole and ten years’ exclusion from public affairs.

Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, detention could last up to five years for offences punishable by life imprisonment, extendable by one year for certain homicide charges. Constitutional Court decision no. 10/2021 declared unlimited pre-trial detention for life-punishable offences unconstitutional with effect from 30 September 2021, stating that strict criminal supervision should suffice after the statutory maximum, without specifying a maximum period. The applicant complains under Article 5 § 3 that his pre-trial detention was unreasonably long and lacked adequate justification.

The application was lodged against Albania by ten Albanian nationals, represented by E. Syziu, a lawyer in Tirana. The Government was represented by O. Moçka, General State Advocate. The applicants complained of an alleged violation of their right of access to the Supreme Court.

On 2 September 1995, the Commission for the Restitution and Compensation of Property recognised the applicants’ inherited property rights over a 5,878 sq. m plot in Tirana. It restored part of the plot measuring 2,999.6 sq. m, awarded compensation for 2,501.4 sq. m, and granted a right of first refusal over 615 sq. m. The decision’s reasoning stated that the property had an actual surface area of 7,600 sq. m. In 1996, title to the restored property was entered in the land register.

On 12 September 2007, the Immovable Property Registration Office of Tirana informed the applicants that an inconsistency between the restored plot and the accompanying map prevented it from taking further action. On 12 March 2008, the applicants asked the Agency for the Restitution and Compensation of Property, successor to the Commission, to correct the inconsistency. On 18 March 2008, the Agency told them to apply to its regional office under Article 120 of the Code of Administrative Procedure. They did so on 4 April 2008. On 14 November 2008, the regional office dismissed the request for lack of jurisdiction, stating that under section 18 of the Property Act the power to amend the 1995 decision rested with the Agency. On 25 November 2008, the applicants applied to the Agency’s central office. Those proceedings lasted more than three years and were suspended pending Constitutional Court decisions of 2010 and 2011.

On 7 November 2011, the Agency held that the Commission’s decisions were no longer subject to administrative review because it lacked jurisdiction, as they were considered quasi-judicial. It also stated that the 2008 regional-office decision had been lawful, since the central office had then had power to review former commission decisions, but that this jurisdiction had been removed after a 2010 Constitutional Court ruling.

The applicants then brought a civil action in the Tirana District Court, seeking to quash the Agency’s decision and rectify the 1995 Commission decision. On 3 December 2012, the District Court partly allowed the claim. Relying on an expert report, it found that the documents establishing the ancestor’s property rights referred to an outdated unit of measurement. It ordered rectification of the 1995 decision by adding the word “old” to the unit of measurement in the operative part.

The Agency and the State Advocate’s office appealed, arguing inter alia that the claim was time-barred. On 26 June 2014, the Tirana Court of Appeal upheld the District Court’s judgment. The correction was entered in the land register.

On 6 April 2022, the Supreme Court reversed the lower courts’ judgment in camera and dismissed the applicants’ claim as time-barred. It held that the applicants should have brought proceedings within 30 days of becoming aware of the discrepancy between the 1995 decision and the accompanying map. Even assuming they had not been aware in 1995, the 30-day time-limit began when the IPRO informed them of the inconsistency. It further found that, rather than lodging an administrative complaint, they should have brought the matter directly before the domestic courts. On 12 October 2022, the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicants’ constitutional complaint as being of a fourth-instance nature.

Article 120 of the Code of Administrative Procedure allows correction of clerical errors or manifest inaccuracies without altering substance and sets no statutory time-limit. Section 18 of the 2004 Property Act, as amended by law no. 9684/2007, provided that appeals against decisions of former local commissions could be lodged with the Agency’s central office by the expropriated party or the State Advocate’s office, and the expropriated party could then appeal to the Tirana District Court within 30 days of notification.

The applicants are five Greek nationals whose properties in Amaliada were expropriated. On 31 August 2018 they lodged an application against the Hellenic Republic. The application concerned compensation payable after the expropriation of their properties.

By a joint ministerial decision issued on 11 February 2008 and published in the Official Government Gazette on 25 February 2008, the expropriation of the applicants’ properties was ordered for the construction of a highway. On 24 February 2009 the Greek State applied for determination of the provisional compensation payable. Hearings took place on 15, 29 and 30 October 2009.

By judgment no. 53/2010 of 26 April 2010, the Amaliada Court of First Instance fixed provisional unitary compensation amounts. For the first applicant, it awarded EUR 10.08 per sq. m for plot no. 201 and EUR 5.42 per sq. m for plot no. 206. For the second applicant, it awarded EUR 4.74 per sq. m for plot no. 300 and EUR 4.50 per sq. m for plot no. 305. For the third applicant, it awarded EUR 101.08 per sq. m for plot no. 078. For the fourth applicant, it awarded EUR 101.08 per sq. m for plot no. 079. For the fifth applicant, it awarded EUR 4.74 per sq. m for plots nos. 316 and 318, and EUR 4.28 per sq. m for plot no. 321. The calculation used property values at the dates of the first-instance hearings. The court also held that the non-expropriated parts of the properties would derive a special benefit from the works because they would have access to the highway.

On 20 October 2010 the Greek State applied for determination of the final compensation. After adjournments on 12 May 2011 and 21 March 2013, the hearing took place on 15 January 2015.

The applicants took several steps concerning the alleged benefit to their remaining properties. On 19 January 2011 the first applicant lodged a counterclaim seeking determination of final compensation and challenging the presumption of benefit, and submitted a written request to intervene. At the hearing of 15 January 2015, the first, second and fifth applicants orally requested leave to intervene and challenged the presumption of benefit. The third and fourth applicants challenged the presumption by written submissions filed at that hearing. Separately, on 14 October 2010 the fifth applicant lodged an application seeking determination of final compensation and challenging the presumption of benefit.

By judgment no. 78/2016 of 31 May 2016, the Patras Court of Appeal dismissed as inadmissible the applicants’ claims regarding the presumption of benefit. It held that the first applicant had not complied with Article 33 § 7 of Law no. 2971/2001, which required a challenge within six months of the provisional compensation determination of 26 April 2010. It further held that the oral intervention requests by the first, second and fifth applicants and the written submissions of the third and fourth applicants sought to extend the scope of the final compensation application contrary to national procedural rules. It also found that the fifth applicant’s claims lacked factual details about the affected parts of his properties.

The Patras Court of Appeal then fixed final unitary compensation amounts: EUR 8 per sq. m for plot no. 201 and EUR 2.60 for plot no. 206 (first applicant); EUR 2 per sq. m for plots nos. 300 and 305 (second applicant); EUR 6.50 for plot no. 078 (third applicant); EUR 6.50 for plot no. 079 (fourth applicant); and EUR 2.50 for plots nos. 316, 318 and 350 and EUR 2 for plot no. 321 (fifth applicant). It relied on Article 17 § 2 (c) of the Greek Constitution and Article 13 § 1 (b) of Law no. 2882/2001, under which final compensation is calculated by reference to values at the date of the appellate hearing where more than one year has passed since the provisional-compensation hearing. It also referred to property-value depreciation from 2009 onward. As to plots nos. 078 and 079, they had been recorded within settlement boundaries, an error later rectified, aligning their unit prices with the other plots.

The applicants appealed on points of law, arguing that the appellate court should have used the provisional-compensation hearing date, not the date of its own hearing, as the critical date for final compensation, which resulted in lower awards. They also argued that the appellate court had wrongly dismissed their claims about the presumption of benefit.

By judgment no. 2062/2017, final on 1 March 2018, the Court of Cassation examined the arguments on the merits and dismissed them. It ruled that the relevant constitutional and statutory provisions applied regardless of increases or decreases in property values between the two hearings. It upheld the appellate findings on the presumption of benefit and also held that, in any event, all applicants’ claims lacked sufficient factual details as to the parts of their properties allegedly not benefiting from the works.

The applicants complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, reiterating the arguments made before the domestic courts.

The applicant, Oliver Fišić, a Croatian national born in 1968 and living in Brašina, complained that he had been denied access to a tribunal concerning a mayoral decision in a public tender in which he had participated as a bidder. He was represented by B. Radan; the Government by Š. Stažnik.

On 15 March 2017 the mayor of Župa dubrovačka ordered a committee to organise a tender for the lease of public areas for vending stands. The tender, published on 20 March 2017, set eligibility criteria, lease duration, minimum bid amounts and the submission deadline; the best bidder would be selected under the municipality’s Decision. The applicant bid 16 HRK per square metre per day for a vending stand in Brašina; another bidder, N.P., bid 11 HRK for the same location. On 5 April 2017 the committee found both bids timely and compliant. Because the bids differed, it decided under section 13 of the municipality’s Decision that N.P., the previous lessee, be offered the lease at the higher price submitted by the applicant. On 21 April N.P. agreed to pay that higher price. On 26 April 2017 the mayor accepted N.P.’s bid and concluded a lease with her. The applicant objected that the mayoral decision was unlawful. On 27 July 2017 the Municipal Council dismissed the objection, emphasising that section 13 gave priority to previous lessees to ensure legal certainty. On 28 July 2017 the municipality, represented by the mayor, concluded a lease with N.P.

The applicant brought an administrative action in the Split Administrative Court challenging the 26 April 2017 mayoral decision. He argued that misapplication of section 13 disadvantaged him vis-à-vis a lower bidder; that priority should apply only if two identical bids were submitted; and that section 13 did not allow the previous lessee to disclose or match the highest bid. On 9 April 2019 the Split Administrative Court set aside the Municipal Council’s decision of 27 July 2017 but upheld the mayoral decision of 26 April 2017. It noted that, under a practice direction of 28 April 2008, acts granting leases of public areas were administrative acts subject to administrative judicial review; no appeal lay against individual mayoral acts; the Municipal Council therefore lacked competence. It reviewed the mayoral decision and found the facts properly established and the law properly applied. The applicant appealed, repeating his arguments and adding that, had section 13 allowed the previous lessee to disclose or match the highest bid, he would never have submitted a bid. On 24 September 2020 the High Administrative Court quashed the Split judgment and declared the administrative action inadmissible. It held, pursuant to its decision of 26 January 2015 in a specific tender procedure, that decisions on leases of public areas were not administrative acts but acts of property management outside administrative judicial review.

On 1 April 2021 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint alleging violations of fair trial, equality before the law, and entrepreneurial and market freedom, relying on the State’s obligation to ensure equal status of entrepreneurs. On 22 December 2021 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint as manifestly ill-founded. It found the restriction on access to a court constitutionally acceptable given the sufficient and relevant reasons provided by the High Administrative Court. That decision was served on 10 January 2022.

Domestically, section 13 of the municipality’s Decision set a priority order for previous lessees, war veterans and related persons, and local residents, with a lease concluded after final selection. A 2008 practice direction treated public-area awards as administrative acts. A 2015 High Administrative Court decision treated such mayoral decisions as property management, and a 2019 Constitutional Court decision found no access-to-court violation. Administrative courts then declared related actions inadmissible between 2016 and 2020. In a 2020 decision, the Constitutional Court held that judicial protection had to be ensured for all individual acts of public authorities. From 2018 onwards, some administrative courts again treated grants of use of public areas as administrative acts and examined cases on the merits.

The applicants, Háttér Társaság and Amnesty International Hungary, are Hungarian organisations based in Budapest, represented by Mr Tordai. They complained of violations of their rights to freedom of expression and a fair trial arising from decisions of Hungary’s National Election Commission (“NEC”) fining them for campaigning for invalid ballots in a national referendum.

In July 2021 the Hungarian Government organised a referendum, stated to aim at protecting children’s best interests. It submitted five questions to the NEC. After legal challenges, the President of the Republic announced that the referendum would be held on 3 April 2022 with only the first four questions. The applicant organisations, together with twelve other civil-society organisations, campaigned encouraging voters to cast invalid ballots, arguing that the questions were misleading and promoted homophobic and transphobic policies. The referendum was held on 3 April 2022, the same day as a general election. About 1,700,000 voters cast invalid ballots, roughly 30% of ballots cast. The referendum results were invalid for all four questions because a majority of registered voters did not cast a valid vote.

Following a third-party complaint, the NEC found on 8 April 2022 (decision no. 324/2022) that the first applicant had infringed section 2(1)(e) of Act no. XXXVI of 2013 on Electoral Procedure (“EPA”), the principle of exercising rights in accordance with their purpose, by publishing Facebook posts calling for invalid ballots. The NEC fined it HUF 3,000,000 (about EUR 7,400). It reasoned that voters may cast invalid ballots, but a campaign encouraging this was incompatible with the referendum’s purpose and obstructed the people’s expression of will. On the same day, decision no. 328/2022 found that the applicant organisations operated the website ervenytelenul.hu, which called on voters to “Cast an invalid vote in response to an invalid question” and advised how to mark ballots invalid. The NEC found the same infringement but imposed no fine because the campaign period had ended.

The first applicant sought judicial review of the fine, arguing that referendum campaigns were a crucial forum for public affairs, that encouraging voters to cast a lawful invalid vote fell within highly protected expression, and that its conduct did not violate the purpose of referendum campaigning. In decision no. Kvk.IV.39.419/2022/4 of 13 April 2022, the Kúria rejected the claim without examining the merits, holding that the first applicant had failed to show specific grounds why the NEC’s interpretation was wrong or to identify the precise rights or values allegedly not balanced. Both applicants also challenged decision no. 328/2022, adding that restriction required a specific statutory basis and had to be necessary and proportionate, and that no provision prohibited encouraging invalid votes. In decision no. Kvk.IV.39.420/2022/4 of 13 April 2022, the Kúria dismissed the claim on the same grounds.

Each applicant lodged a constitutional complaint, alleging infringement of freedom of expression under Article IX and fair trial under Article XXVIII of the Fundamental Law. They argued the Kúria failed to adjudicate the merits and ignored their arguments, and that the NEC’s restriction lacked legal basis and was disproportionate. On 22 April 2022, the Constitutional Court rejected the complaints (decisions nos. 3216/2022 and 3217/2022). It held that the fair-trial complaint raised no constitutional issue but challenged legality, and that the Kúria’s examination was a precondition for constitutional review of the expression issue.

The record also notes other NEC decisions of 8 April 2022: decision no. 325/2022 fined the second applicant HUF 3,000,000; decision no. 327/2022 fined the applicants and fourteen other organisations HUF 176,400 each; and decision no. 329/2022 found the Hungarian Civil Liberties Union had breached section 2(1)(e) but imposed no fine. On 15 April 2022, the Kúria overturned those decisions, holding that campaign activity formed part of protected expression, that no explicit statutory restriction existed, and that restrictions required constitutional and statutory grounds.

The applicant, Ersan Taş, is a Turkish national born in 1984 who lives in Istanbul. At the time of the events, he held a Twitter account named “@06melihchina,” followed by more than 55,000 users. The account was a parody account that portrayed jokes about İ.M.G., then mayor of Ankara.

On 24 September 2014, İ.M.G.’s official account on the same platform posted a photo and a mocking statement about K.K., then chairman of the main opposition party. On the same day, the applicant made a comment under that post. His comment included a derisive image pertaining to the President and İ.M.G., accompanied by the statement: “We continue to work and steal tirelessly with our President, God willing” (Cumhurbaşkanımızla birlikte hiç durmadan çalışmaya ve çalmaya devam ediyoruz Allah’ın izniyle).

On 17 December 2014, İ.M.G. filed a criminal complaint against the applicant concerning the content of his comment. On 26 September 2017, the Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance sentenced the applicant to eleven months and twenty days’ imprisonment for insulting the President of the Republic and ten months’ imprisonment for insulting a public official on account of his functions. The Criminal Court suspended the pronouncement of the judgment under Article 231 § 5 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and imposed a five-year supervision period. On 9 November 2017, the Ankara Assize Court dismissed the applicant’s objection, finding that the decision had been made in accordance with procedural and substantial law.

On 20 December 2017, the applicant lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court. Relying on Article 10 of the Convention, he complained, among other things, about his conviction owing to the comment in question. On 29 March 2023, the Constitutional Court found a violation of the applicant’s right to freedom of expression in a judgment grouping similar applications, in accordance with its findings in the Atilla Yazar and Others judgment. To redress the violation, the Constitutional Court ordered a retrial and sent a copy of its judgment to the Criminal Court for the reopening of the criminal proceedings. It also ordered reimbursement of the court fees the applicant had paid before the Criminal Court, as well as his legal representation costs. However, it rejected his just satisfaction claims in respect of non-pecuniary damage. The decision was served on the applicant’s lawyer on 13 July 2023.

On 9 November 2023, the applicant introduced an application before the European Court. On the same day, he lodged a petition with the Criminal Court seeking a retrial to secure implementation of the Constitutional Court’s judgment. On 12 December 2023, the Criminal Court rejected the applicant’s request in a final decision, stating that the Constitutional Court had not yet delivered its decision concerning the applicant’s individual application. On 15 November 2024, the Constitutional Court filed a petition with the Criminal Court requesting information on the retrial proceedings. On 21 November 2024, the Criminal Court informed the Constitutional Court that the retrial proceedings had not been commenced, without providing any reasons.

In his application to the Court, relying on Article 10 of the Convention, the applicant complained that his right to freedom of expression had been breached on account of his conviction and prison sentence, combined with a measure of suspension of the pronouncement of the judgment, owing to a comment he had posted on social media.
001-253232:
Application no. 23441/25 was lodged against Bulgaria with the European Court of Human Rights on 1 August 2025 by A.M., an Uzbek national born in 1981. He was represented by V. Petkov, a lawyer practising in Sofia. Bulgaria is the respondent State.

The applicant arrived in Bulgaria in August 2022 and applied for international protection in October 2022. The State Agency for Refugees (“SAR”) interviewed him and, under an accelerated procedure, rejected the application as manifestly unfounded. The Sofia City Administrative Court (“SCAC”) upheld that decision after he lodged a claim for judicial review.

In December 2022 the applicant lodged a subsequent application for international protection, enclosing an opinion by a psychologist he had consulted. The SAR rejected the application without an examination on the merits. The applicant sought judicial review, and the SCAC again upheld the SAR’s decision.

In April 2023 he lodged a second subsequent application for international protection. He enclosed a report by two forensic medical experts who had examined him and four documents he described as having been issued by the Uzbek authorities. The SAR rejected the application without examining it on the merits. The SCAC set that decision aside after the applicant lodged a judicial review claim. After interviewing the applicant, the SAR dismissed the application. The SCAC upheld that decision, and the Supreme Administrative Court (“SAC”) upheld the SCAC’s judgment on appeal.

In June 2025 the applicant lodged a third subsequent application for international protection. The SAR rejected it without considering it on the merits. The applicant sought judicial review of that decision but later withdrew his claim, and the SCAC discontinued the proceedings. He later stated that he wished to retract the withdrawal. The SCAC directed him to clarify whether that statement was intended as an appeal against the discontinuance. The applicant did not comply, and the discontinuance became final.

In February 2023, while the above applications were being processed, the migration authorities ordered the applicant’s return to Uzbekistan. He sought judicial review, but the SCAC upheld the order and the SAC upheld the SCAC’s judgment on appeal. He later sought to have the SAC proceedings reopened but abandoned that attempt.

In July 2025 the applicant was placed in immigration detention. Separately, after twice attempting to cross illegally into Romania in March and April 2025, he was sentenced in October 2025 to eighteen months’ imprisonment. He remained in prison serving that sentence until June 2026. He was then placed in immigration detention.

The applicant complained under Article 3 of the Convention that the Bulgarian authorities and courts had not properly assessed whether he would face a risk of ill-treatment if removed to Uzbekistan. He alleged that the risk was real and that, if he were removed, this would breach Article 3.
